source: Grossi and Pigozzi (2012) Introduction to Judgment Aggregation (tutorial, citing Kornhauser and Sager 1986/1993)
finding: Original doctrinal paradox: three judges vote on premises p (valid contract), q (breach) and conclusion r (liable iff p and q). Majority on each premise says yes, majority on the conclusion says no. The court's verdict depends on the procedure used.
numbers: 3 judges. Votes (p,q,r): J1 1,1,1; J2 1,0,0; J3 0,1,0. Majority: p=1, q=1, r=0. Premise-based procedure gives liable; conclusion-based gives not liable.
quote: We have no clear understanding of how a court should proceed in cases where the doctrinal paradox arises.
limits: A toy case; the paradox needs a logical link between propositions. It is a fact about the agenda, not about court law only. Kornhauser and Sager's own papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: If our agent votes over attempts on a final answer AND on intermediate claims, the two routes can disagree. Pick the route in code and say which.

source: Grossi and Pigozzi (2012) Introduction to Judgment Aggregation: discursive dilemma (Pettit 2001) and CO2 agenda
finding: Pettit (2001) generalised the paradox to the discursive dilemma: propositionwise majority voting over logically related propositions can give an inconsistent collective set even when every member is consistent.
numbers: Agenda {p, p->q, q}. J1={p,p->q,q}; J2={p,not(p->q),not q}; J3={not p,p->q,not q}. Majority accepts p, p->q and not q: inconsistent.
limits: Shows inconsistency of the pooled set, not wrong answers. No claim about truth.
agent_relevance: Pooling claim-by-claim across attempts can produce a plan no single attempt believes and that contradicts itself. Check consistency of any pooled claim set with code (G5).

source: List and Pettit (2002) Aggregating sets of judgments: an impossibility result (as stated in Grossi and Pigozzi 2012, Thm 1, from Dietrich and List)
finding: First impossibility theorem of judgment aggregation. For agendas that are non-simple and evenly negatable (e.g. {p, q, p and q} with negations), an aggregation function that accepts all consistent profiles (universal domain) and is systematic is dictatorial. List and Pettit's original used anonymity; the Dietrich-List form is this one.
numbers: Theorem 1: for such agendas, f satisfies U (universal domain) and SYS (systematicity) iff f is a dictatorship. A proof, no data.
limits: Read through the survey, not the 2002 paper itself. Escape routes: restrict profiles, drop systematicity (premise-based rule), accept incomplete outputs.
agent_relevance: No rule that treats every claim identically, takes any mix of attempts and returns a complete consistent set is non-dictatorial. S7 must choose which condition to give up. Dropping systematicity (decide premises by vote, derive the rest) is the usual choice.

source: Grossi and Pigozzi (2012): Nehring's Paretian dilemma and the Bovens-Rabinowicz/List truth-tracking comparison
finding: Premise-based voting tracks truth better than conclusion-based voting under Condorcet assumptions, but it can overturn a unanimous verdict on the conclusion (Nehring's Paretian dilemma). Nehring shows only dictatorial rules satisfy independence, monotonicity and unanimity on the conclusion.
numbers: Competence p>0.5 per proposition and independence give majority reliability rising with group size. Paretian dilemma: three judges, three premises (duty, negligence, causation); each judge rejects one different premise so all reject liability, yet the premise-wise majorities accept all three (as described in the survey).
limits: Normative force of the Pareto criterion depends on shared self-interest versus shared responsibility. Premise independence assumed.
agent_relevance: If every attempt rejects the final answer but premise votes accept all premises, the program must not silently override. Flag it as a conflict and trigger a check (G1) rather than deciding by vote.

source: List (2005) The probability of inconsistencies in complex collective decisions, Social Choice and Welfare
finding: Computes how often propositionwise majority is inconsistent for the conjunctive agenda (R iff P and Q) as group size n grows. Under impartial culture the chance converges to 0.25; under small departures it converges to 1 or to 0 depending on the profile mix. The paradox is likely under plausible conditions.
numbers: Table 3 (R iff P and Q). Impartial culture (all four P,Q patterns 0.25): n=3 0.0938, n=11 0.2157, n=101 0.2500. Scenario 3 (pTT=0.3, pTF=pFT=0.25, pFF=0.2): 0.1125 at n=3, 0.4979 at n=31, 0.9754 at n=501, 0.9999 at n=1501. Scenario 8 (pTT=pTF=pFT=0.33, pFF=0.01): 0.2156 at n=3, 0.9757 at n=51. Proposition 3: probability tends to 1 if pTT+pTF>1/2, pTT+pFT>1/2 and pTT<1/2.
limits: Individuals assumed independent of each other; for the epistemic part, each person's judgments on P and on Q also assumed independent. High within-person dependence sharply cuts the paradox.
agent_relevance: More voters can make inconsistency MORE likely, not less. Pooling many attempts over claim sets is not safe by default; a consistency check in code is needed, not more samples.

source: List (2005) Probability of inconsistencies: truth-tracking of premise-based (PBP) and conclusion-based (CBP) procedures
finding: With independent voters of competence p,q>0.5 on the premises, the premise-based procedure reaches the right decision on the conclusion with probability tending to 1 as n grows. The conclusion-based procedure tends to 0 for the right reasons unless competence is high (pq>0.5), and does badly when both premises are true.
numbers: Proposition 5 / Table 6: PBP to 1 whenever p,q>0.5. CBP right-for-right-reasons to 0 unless pq>0.5. If P and Q are not both true, CBP reaches the correct decision regardless of reasons faster than PBP. If a voter is right on P iff right on Q, PBP and CBP always coincide and no inconsistency occurs.
limits: Needs independent errors across people AND across premises. The perfect-dependence limit removes the paradox but also removes any gain from splitting.
agent_relevance: Decomposing a task into sub-claims and voting on those beats voting on the final answer only if sub-claim errors are independent (G4). Model sub-claim errors are often correlated (see a25).

source: List (2008) Group knowledge and group rationality: a judgment aggregation perspective (Episteme), Condorcet jury theorem tables
finding: Restates the Condorcet jury theorem with explicit competence (r>1/2) and independence conditions, then compares majority, dictatorial, unanimity, conclusion-based and premise-based rules. Majority beats dictatorship and unanimity on both positive and negative reliability when voters are independent and truth-biased. Unanimity helps only if false positives are very costly.
numbers: Illustration with r=0.54 per voter (curves, group size on the axis). Conclusion-based rule: unless premise reliability r exceeds the k-th root of 0.5 (0.71 for k=2 premises, 0.79 for k=3), positive reliability on the conclusion goes to 0 as the group grows and negative reliability to 1. A dictator gets all k premises right with probability r^k. Specialisation: individual r=0.52 needs r*=0.5281 after specialisation to break even (k=2); r=0.6 needs 0.6393; r=0.75 needs 0.8315.
quote: Each group member's judgments are mutually independent
limits: Curves are model outputs, not data. Independence and equal competence assumed. The paper itself states the independence condition as required.
agent_relevance: Voting beats picking one attempt only under independence and above-chance competence. Where per-attempt accuracy on the right answer is below 0.5, more votes lock in the wrong answer (G4).

source: List (2003) A possibility theorem on aggregation over multiple interconnected propositions, Mathematical Social Sciences
finding: Escape route from the List-Pettit impossibility: if individual judgments are unidimensionally aligned (members can be ordered so each proposition is accepted by an interval of them, like single-peakedness) then propositionwise majority is consistent. Completeness can fail only in edge cases.
numbers: Theorem 2: aggregation functions on the restricted domain of unidimensionally aligned profiles, with anonymity and systematicity, give consistent (almost complete) outputs. The paper states Black's median-voter analogy.
limits: Needs a one-dimensional ordering of views; deliberation may create it, but nothing guarantees it. Theorem details read in outline only.
agent_relevance: If attempts differ along one axis, claim-wise vote is safe. A program can test for such alignment before using claim-wise vote.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) Condorcet's jury theorem (statement and extensions: Berend-Paroush, Romaniega Sancho, Caplan)
finding: Classical theorem: n independent voters each correct with probability p; if p>1/2 the majority accuracy rises toward 1 as n grows; if p<1/2 it falls toward 0 and one voter is best. Heterogeneous competences handled by Berend and Paroush (1998). Random draws of competence from an unbiased distribution fail the theorem almost surely (Romaniega Sancho 2022, as stated by the page).
numbers: n=3, p=0.8 gives majority accuracy 0.896. Near p=1/2 the gain grows about with sqrt((2n+1)/pi) times (p-1/2).
limits: Encyclopedia secondary source via a summarising fetch; the page says empirical validity is an open question. Original Condorcet 1785 not opened.
agent_relevance: Gain depends on where p sits relative to 1/2. Per-item p varies, so on hard items the vote can reverse. Treat agreement as a hint, not proof (G4).

source: Condorcet (1785); Ladha (1992) correlated voters; Dietrich (2008) premises not simultaneously justified (background, not opened)
finding: From memory: Ladha 1992 shows the theorem can survive mild positive correlation between voters, but a strongly correlated group can do worse than one voter; the condition ties average pairwise correlation to competence. Dietrich 2008 argues independence and competence cannot both be justified for the same problem description.
numbers: No numbers verified this session. Do not cite figures from this line.
limits: Not opened; recalled from memory. Must be re-read before use. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Underlines G4: independence is the weak link and fails more for one model's samples.

source: Genest and Zidek (1986) Combining probability distributions: a critique and an annotated bibliography, Statistical Science (background, not opened)
finding: From memory: review of opinion-pooling rules. Linear opinion pool (weighted average) has the marginalisation property but is not externally Bayesian and does not preserve independence. Logarithmic (geometric) pool is externally Bayesian but lacks marginalisation. No rule has all desirable properties.
numbers: No numbers verified; full text could not be fetched (Project Euclid returned empty content).
limits: Not opened; the property list is from memory and must be confirmed against the paper.
agent_relevance: S7 pooling rule is a design choice: arithmetic mean for robustness, geometric or logit average for combining independent evidence. Test, do not assume.

source: Dietrich and List (2016) Probabilistic opinion pooling (background, not opened)
finding: From memory: extends pooling to logically linked propositions. Linear pooling is characterised by independence and unanimity preservation; the same impossibility structure as judgment aggregation appears.
numbers: No numbers verified.
limits: Not opened; recalled. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Probability pooling over exclusive answers should be done in code with normalisation (G5); the pool type is a parameter to measure.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models (ICLR 2023)
finding: Sample many reasoning paths, take the majority final answer. This is Condorcet-style aggregation over one model's samples. Gains over greedy chain of thought across arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks.
numbers: Absolute gains in points: GSM8K +17.9, SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9. Unweighted majority gives accuracy very similar to the normalised probability-weighted sum, because path probabilities are close; unnormalised weighting is worse; weighted average is much worse.
limits: Same model, so samples are not independent (G4). Gains shrink on commonsense tasks. Answers must be extractable as discrete strings.
agent_relevance: Vote over final answers is cheap and works as a hint. Simple majority is as good as fancy weighting. Do not let it stand as proof.

source: Du et al. (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: 3 agents with 2 rounds of debate raised accuracy over a single agent, reflection and simple multi-agent majority, on arithmetic, GSM8K, chess and facts.
numbers: Table 1: Arithmetic: single 67.0+-4.7, reflection 72.1+-4.5, majority 69.0+-4.6, debate 81.8+-2.3. GSM8K: single 77.0+-4.2, reflection 75.0+-4.3, majority 81.0+-3.9, debate 85.0+-3.5. Table 2: Biographies 66.0 to 73.8; MMLU 63.9 to 71.1; chess validity 29.3 to 45.2. Mixed models: 20 GSM8K problems, Bard 11, chatGPT 14, joint debate 17.
limits: Small samples. Later work (a15, a16) finds majority voting accounts for most of the gain. Same-model agents.
agent_relevance: Debate is an expensive form of pooling. Its gain over plain majority on GSM8K (85.0 vs 81.0) overlaps in error bars.

source: Choi, Zhu, Li (2025) Debate or Vote: which yields better decisions in multi-agent LLMs?
finding: Splits multi-agent debate into majority voting and debate. Majority voting alone accounts for most of the gain. Proves debate is a martingale over agents' belief in the correct answer, so debate alone does not raise expected correctness. Gives a Dirichlet model of voting success.
numbers: Table 1, Qwen2.5-7B, average over 7 benchmarks: single agent 0.7205; decentralised MAD T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; sparse MAD T=2 0.7330; centralised MAD T=2 0.6551; majority voting 0.7691. Arithmetic: single 0.8140, MAD T=2 0.7600, voting 0.9900. Theorem 1: P(vote correct) lower bound 1-exp(-N*margin term) when N>K/2. MAD-oracle (bias updates toward truth) lifts MMLU formal logic from 0.5000 to 0.6825 at T=5 but needs ground truth.
limits: Mostly 7-8B models; a Qwen2.5-32B check in section 6. Dirichlet model assumes a fixed belief vector per agent.
agent_relevance: Spend budget on independent samples plus a vote, not rounds of discussion. Revision after seeing peers needs an external signal such as a test result (G2), not a majority.

source: Smit et al. (2024) Should we be going MAD? A look at multi-agent debate strategies for LLMs (ICML 2024)
finding: Benchmarks several debate protocols against self-consistency, ensemble refinement and a single agent. Debate does not reliably beat self-consistency or ensembling over multiple reasoning paths. Some protocols (e.g. Multi-Persona) improve after hyperparameter tuning, so debate is sensitive to settings.
numbers: A self-consistency row in the results table shows 0.60, 0.74, 0.78, 0.46 on four datasets; exact dataset mapping not verified.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and part of the results were read. Accuracy cells are partial.
agent_relevance: Debate adds hyperparameters, cost and a conformity risk without a reliable edge over sampling and voting. Keep voting in code (G5).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Rethinking the bounds of LLM reasoning: are multi-agent discussions the key?
finding: A single agent with a strong prompt (a demonstration or a detailed question description) reaches nearly the best multi-agent discussion performance on many reasoning tasks. Discussion beats a single agent only when the prompt has no demonstration.
numbers: Figure 1 (FOLIO-wiki): single agent with a demonstration reaches the upper bound of all tested discussion frameworks. No further exact numbers extracted.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and Figure 1 text were read. Figures not seen.
agent_relevance: A better prompt may replace a crowd. Test a strong single-attempt baseline before adding voters.

source: Li et al. (2024) More agents is all you need (Agent Forest), TMLR
finding: Plain sampling-and-voting improves accuracy with ensemble size across tasks. Relative gains are larger for weaker models and, within limits, harder tasks. A small model can overtake a larger one.
numbers: Gains in points: GSM8K +12 to +24, MATH +6 to +10, Chess +1 to +4, MMLU +5 to +11, HumanEval +4 to +9. Llama2-13B with ensemble 59% GSM8K vs Llama2-70B single 54%. Relative gains: GSM8K 69/37/16% and MATH 200/120/34% for Llama2-13B/Llama2-70B/GPT-3.5-Turbo. Synthetic task (GPT-3.5, up to 40 samples): gains rise then fall with inherent difficulty, largest at I=100 and 200, smaller at I=400.
limits: Same-model samples; chess gains only 1-4 points. Gains taper at very hard difficulty, which fits the Condorcet low-competence regime.
agent_relevance: Voting helps most in the middle band where p is just above 0.5. On items where p<0.5 it will hurt.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing judges with juries: evaluating LLM generations with a Panel of LLM evaluators (PoLL)
finding: A panel of three smaller judges from different model families (Command R, Haiku, GPT-3.5), pooled by max vote (binary) or average (1-5 scores), correlates better with humans than a single GPT-4 judge, shows less self-preference bias, and costs over seven times less.
numbers: Chatbot Arena rank agreement with the crowd leaderboard: PoLL Pearson 0.917, Kendall 0.778; GPT-4 0.817 / 0.667; Haiku 0.883 / 0.722; GPT-3.5 0.883 / 0.730; Command R 0.817 / 0.676. Spread of judge deviation from humans on multi-hop QA: PoLL sd 2.2, GPT-3.5 sd 6.1. One single-hop kappa row: PoLL 0.763, 0.906, 0.867.
limits: Only one three-judge panel; ties for 1-5 scores forced averaging. Largest bias when a model judges itself.
agent_relevance: Diverse judges pooled in code beat one strong judge. Supports G4 (different families) and G5 (judge sees no authorship).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the silicon crowd: LLM ensemble prediction capabilities rival human crowd accuracy (Study 1)
finding: Median of 12 LLM forecasts on 31 binary Metaculus questions is not statistically different from a crowd of 925 humans, and equivalent within a medium-size bound. LLM predictions show acquiescence bias (mean above 50% although 14 of 31 questions resolved yes).
numbers: LLM crowd Brier 0.20 (sd 0.12) vs human crowd 0.19 (sd 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Better than the 0.25 chance benchmark, t(30)=-2.35, p=0.026. 1,007 forecasts. Mean LLM prediction 57.35% (sd 20.93). Single models: GPT-4 0.15, GPT-4 with Bing 0.16, Bard 0.19, Claude 2 0.21, Llama-2-70B 0.25, Coral 0.38.
limits: 31 questions, one 3-month window. Best single model GPT-4 (0.15) beat the crowd median, so the pool is not shown better than the best member.
agent_relevance: Median over several different-family models is a cheap forecast pool. Acquiescence is a shared bias a mean cannot remove.

source: Schoenegger et al. (2024) Study 2: LLMs updating on the human median forecast
finding: Giving GPT-4 and Claude 2 the human median improved their Brier scores, but simply averaging human and machine forecasts did better than letting the model update.
numbers: GPT-4: 0.17 (sd 0.13) to 0.14 (sd 0.11), p=0.003. Claude 2: 0.22 (sd 0.19) to 0.15 (sd 0.14), p<0.001. 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts. Abstract: accuracy improved by 17 to 28 percent, but less than simple averaging.
limits: Single question set. The updating model sees an anchor, so it is not an independent voter.
agent_relevance: Pool by averaging in code rather than asking a model to update toward the pool (G5, sycophancy).

source: Halawi et al. (2024) Approaching human-level forecasting with language models: ensembling results
finding: Trimmed mean of 6 base forecasts was the best of five aggregators on validation; universal self-consistency (asking a model to merge) did no better than no ensemble.
numbers: Validation Brier: mean 0.1656, median 0.1651, geometric mean 0.1655, trimmed mean 0.1649, USC 0.1691, no ensemble 0.1676, human crowd 0.1600. Test set: random 0.250, human crowd 0.149, best pretrained model GPT-4-1106 0.208.
limits: Differences between numeric aggregators are about 0.001 to 0.002 Brier, likely inside noise. Only 6 forecasts per question.
agent_relevance: The numeric aggregator (mean, median, trimmed) matters little. A model-written merge step may be worse than a number rule.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents enhances large language model capabilities
finding: Layers of different LLMs, each seeing earlier answers, reach 65.1% AlpacaEval 2.0 LC win rate (abstract) vs 57.5% for GPT-4 Omni, using only open models.
numbers: 65.1% vs 57.5% in the abstract; the body text states 65.8% for the final MoA.
limits: Aggregator is a model, not a rule; benchmark may reward length. The two stated numbers (65.1 and 65.8) differ in the paper itself.
agent_relevance: The aggregator is a model that sees all answers, which conflicts with G5. See the next entry for a counter-result.

source: Li et al. (2025) Rethinking mixture-of-agents: is mixing different LLMs beneficial? (Self-MoA)
finding: Aggregating many samples from the single best model (Self-MoA) beats mixing different models in many settings; mixing adds diversity but pulls in lower-quality answers (a quality-diversity trade-off).
numbers: Self-MoA +6.6 points over Mixed-MoA on AlpacaEval 2.0 and +3.8 on average across MMLU, CRUX and MATH. Task-specific models in Self-MoA beat Mixed-MoA by 0.17% and 0.35% in one comparison.
limits: Contests Wang 2024; depends on task and on the quality spread of proposers.
agent_relevance: Diversity across families helps independence but costs accuracy if the other models are weaker. Do not assume heterogeneous beats best-single; measure.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated errors in large language models (ICML 2025)
finding: Large-scale test of the Condorcet independence premise for LLMs. Models agree on wrong answers far more than chance, and more accurate models are more correlated even across providers. Correlated errors make LLM judges inflate weaker models.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 HuggingFace questions; 71 LLMs on 14,042 Helm questions; 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. Agreement when both wrong: mean 0.423 (HuggingFace) and about 0.60 (Helm), vs chance 0.127 and 0.333. 100% of pairs (HF) and 97.5% (Helm) above chance. One Helm pair agrees on 0.9987 of its common errors (about 22% of questions). Provider, architecture, size and accuracy features explain 34% to 62% of the variation.
limits: Multiple-choice only; agreement measured on wrong answers, not independence of correctness itself.
agent_relevance: Mixing providers does not give independent errors. The Condorcet lift from heterogeneous models is smaller than the formula says. Strong support for G4.

source: Lefort et al. (2024) Examining independence in ensemble sentiment analysis: limits of LLMs using the Condorcet jury theorem
finding: Extends the Condorcet theorem to multi-class classification (IWTUB: independent, well-trained, unbiased) and tests bagging of GPT-3.5, DistilRoBERTa and FinBERT on 3-class financial headline sentiment. Bagging gave almost no gain, read as evidence of non-independent errors.
numbers: Table 5: bagging vs best single SFT GPT-3.5: precision +0.01 / +0.00, recall +0.00 / +0.01, F1 -0.01 / -0.01 (two bagging setups). Random classifier 0.33; non-fine-tuned GPT-4 about 0.47-0.49; FinBERT 0.44-0.46; SFT GPT-3.5 0.51-0.54. About 65,000 Bloomberg headlines; classes 31/27/42%.
limits: One domain, one dataset, three models, not peer reviewed. Non-independence is inferred from confusion matrices, not a formal test.
agent_relevance: When ensemble gain is about 0, suspect shared errors, not a broken vote. Measure error correlation before paying for more voters.

source: Confidence-credibility aware weighted ensembles of small LLMs for emotion detection (2025)
finding: Weighted ensembles of small LLMs reported to outperform large LLMs on emotion detection (title only; numbers not read).
numbers: Not verified.
limits: Marked unopened because the numbers were not read.
agent_relevance: Possible later source for weighted vote versus plain vote.
